draft_context.description: Macworld Apple’s 2026 Watch lineup is now on sale, with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 joining the Apple Watch SE 3. That makes this a reasonable time to buy if you want the latest features. If price matters more, compare the new models with discounted Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock – or wait for the October and Black Friday sales. The SE 3 remains the least expensive option in Apple’s current lineup, but it’s also the oldest as it was introduced in September 2025. If you don’t need a watch immediately, it’s worth considering the major sales events that follow Apple’s launch. Retailers consistently offer their biggest Apple Watch discounts during Amazon Prime Day (July and October) and Black Friday in November. During Prime Day in June 2026, for example, we saw discounts ranging from $50 to $120 on current models. In this guide, we’ll explain whether you should buy an Apple Watch now or wait, the best times of year to find the biggest discounts, and how to avoid paying full price just before a new model arrives. Read our Macworld’s Best Apple Watch guide for more buying advice. Should I buy an Apple Watch now? At a glance Watch Apple Watch SE 3 (Best Value) Apple Watch Series 12 (Best for Most) Apple Watch Ultra 4 (Best for Adventurers) Advice Buy for value Buy for health features Buy for battery life and outdoor features Starting Price $249/£219 $399/£369 $799/£749 Key health and safety features Heart-rate alerts, sleep tracking, temperature sensing, Fall Detection SE 3 features, plus ECG, Blood Oxygen, hypertension alerts, more frequent heart-rate and HRV readings, and Readiness Series 12 health features, plus dive features and satellite Emergency SOS Battery Life Up to 18 hours Up to 24 hours; 38 hours in Low Power Mode Up to 50 hours; 84 in Low Power Mode Best For Budget-conscious users who want core features and iPhone integration Everyday users wanting the best balance of features, health tracking, and price Athletes, hikers, and divers needing maximum durability, GPS, and battery life Buy an Apple Watch now if… Mahmoud Itani / Foundry The Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now on sale alongside the SE 3 and there are no new models expected. Buy now if you need a watch soon or the model you want meets your needs at a price you’re happy to pay. The Series 12 is the best everyday choice, the SE 3 is the best value, and the Ultra 4 makes sense if you need its longer battery life or outdoor features. A discounted Series 11 or Ultra 3 could also be worth buying if you don’t need the latest additions. You should consider buying now if: Your current Apple Watch cannot run watchOS 27, or its battery no longer lasts long enough for your needs. You’re buying your first Apple Watch or upgrading from a much older model. The current watches offer substantial improvements in displays, performance, health tracking and battery life. You want the Series 12 or Ultra 4’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate and HRV readings, and Readiness score. Live Rewind and Siri Recap are due in beta later in 2026 , so don’t count on using those immediately. You would benefit from the Ultra 4’s up to 50-hour battery life, satellite communication or specialist outdoor features. You need a watch before a trip or event, or you find a worthwhile discount on a model that suits you. Don’t buy an Apple Watch now if… The main reason to wait now is price : retailers may discount the new models during October sales and Black Friday. You may want to wait or choose a different model if: You want the lowest possible price and are happy to wait for the next major sale. Compare any Series 12 or Ultra 4 offer with remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock. You already own a Series 10 or 11 and do not need the Series 12’s new health sensing features. Its quoted everyday battery life remains 24 hours. You own an Ultra 3 and its 42-hour battery life and outdoor features already meet your needs. The Ultra 4’s 50-hour rating is its clearest reason to upgrade. You are considering a used watch that cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 8, SE 2 and original Ultra, along with older models, miss out on the latest major software update. You use an Android phone. Apple Watch requires an iPhone. You are considering the SE 3 but need ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring or the new Health Sensing System. Choose the Series 12 instead. Should I buy the Apple Watch Series 12? Price When Reviewed: $399 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $389.99 View Deal $399 View Deal $399 View Deal $399.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Should you buy: Buy The Apple Watch Series 12 is the best choice for most people. Starting at $399/£369 – the same starting price as the Series 11 – it combines Apple’s advanced health features with a smaller, lighter design than the Ultra 4. Its new Health Sensing System measures heart rate every five seconds and heart-rate variability more frequently, providing data for a new Readiness score. The S11 chip also supports Audio Intelligence features, although Live Rewind and Siri Recap are due to arrive in beta later in 2026. Apple still rates everyday battery life at up to 24 hours, the same as Series 11. Outdoor workout tracking lasts longer, however, and a 15-minute charge now provides up to 12 hours of use, compared with around eight hours for Series 11. Aluminum models also gain a tougher Ceramic Shield 2 display. Buy the Apple Watch Series 12 if: You’re buying your first Apple Watch or upgrading from a much older model and want the best everyday option. You want the new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate and HRV measurements, and Readiness score. You want advanced features missing from the SE 3, including ECG, Blood Oxygen monitoring and hypertension notifications. You prefer a lighter watch with two size choices over the larger Ultra 4. Don’t buy the Apple Watch Series 12 if: You own a Series 10 or 11 that still meets your needs. The new health features may not justify the cost of upgrading, and Apple’s 24-hour everyday battery rating has not changed. You can get a Series 11 at a meaningful discount and don’t need the new health sensing or upcoming Audio Intelligence features. You mainly want fitness tracking, notifications and basic safety features. The SE 3 costs $150/£150 less. You need more than a day of battery life, satellite communication or specialist outdoor features. Consider the Ultra 4 instead. Our verdict: This is the Apple Watch we’d recommend to most people buying a new watch today. Its new health sensing features make it a more substantial upgrade than the Series 11 was, while the starting price has stayed the same. Owners of recent watches should weigh those additions against the cost: a discounted Series 11 – or keeping the watch they already have – may be the better value. Should I buy the Apple Watch SE 3? Price When Reviewed: $249 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $249 View Deal $249 View Deal $249.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Should you buy : Buy The Apple Watch SE 3 is the best-value Apple Watch in the lineup and the model we’d recommend for most iPhone users. Announced in September 2025, it brought many features that were previously reserved for Apple’s premium watches, including an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging and the S10 chip used in the Series 11 and Ultra 3. If you don’t need Apple’s most advanced health sensors, the SE 3 delivers almost everything that makes the Apple Watch great at a much lower price. It starts at $249 / £219, although we’ve already seen it discounted to $199 during major sales. The SE 3 also supports Siri AI in watchOS 27 when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone. Siri AI is currently in beta and rolling out in English. The SE 3 does not support the separate Audio Intelligence features coming to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, including Live Rewind and Siri Recap. Buy the Apple Watch SE 3 if: You want the best-value Apple Watch. You’re buying your first smartwatch. You mainly want fitness tracking, notifications and Apple’s core smartwatch features. You want safety features such as Fall Detection, Crash Detection and heart-rate alerts. You’re buying for a child or older family member, particularly the cellular model. Don’t buy the Apple Watch SE 3 if: You need ECG or blood oxygen monitoring, which are only available on the Series 12 and Ultra 4. You want the brightest display and most premium design—the SE 3 still has thicker bezels than the flagship models. You need longer battery life. The SE 3 is rated for 18 hours, compared with 24 hours for the Series 12. You’re happy to spend more for Apple’s most advanced health and fitness features. Our verdict : The Apple Watch SE 3 is an outstanding budget smartwatch. Its always-on display, S10 processor, fast charging and improved health features make it a huge step up from the SE 2. Unless you specifically need ECG, blood oxygen monitoring or the longer battery life of the Series 11, the SE 3 is the Apple Watch we’d recommend to most buyers. Read our full Apple Watch SE 3 (40mm) review Should I buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4? Price When Reviewed: $799 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price $779.99 View Deal $799 View Deal $799.99 View Deal $819 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Should you buy : Yes The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is Apple’s most capable watch, aimed at endurance athletes, hikers, divers and anyone who regularly spends more than a day away from a charger. It starts at $799/£749, the same starting price as the Ultra 3, and retains the 49mm titanium case, bright display, dual-frequency GPS, satellite communication and diving support. Battery life is the strongest reason to choose the new model. Apple rates the Ultra 4 for up to 50 hours of normal use, up from 42 hours on Ultra 3, or 84 hours in Low Power Mode , up from 72. Its new Extended Workout modes can track outdoor activity for up to 25 hours with full GPS and heart-rate readings, or up to 45 hours in Max Extended Workout mode. Like the Series 12, it gains the new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate and HRV readings, and a Readiness score. Its S11 chip supports Audio Intelligence, although Live Rewind and Siri Recap are due in beta later in 2026. Buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4 if: You want the longest battery life available on an Apple Watch, particularly for travel, long shifts or time away from a charger. You need extended outdoor workout tracking, precision dual-frequency GPS or satellite communication. You hike, dive or take part in endurance sports and will use its rugged case, Action button and specialist features. You want the new Health Sensing System in an Ultra watch and are upgrading from a substantially older model. Don’t buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4 if: You already own an Ultra 3 and its 42-hour battery life meets your needs. It retains many of the same outdoor features, including satellite communication and dual-frequency GPS. You find an Ultra 3 at a substantial discount and do not need the Ultra 4’s longer battery life, new health sensing or extended workout modes. You mainly want advanced health features in an everyday watch. The smaller Series 12 has the same new Health Sensing System and S11 chip for half the starting price. You prefer a smaller or lighter watch. The Ultra 4’s 49mm case can feel bulky, especially for sleep tracking. Our verdict: The Ultra 4 is worth buying if you will benefit from its 50-hour battery life, extended workout tracking or outdoor safety features. It also offers the Series 12’s new health sensing in a more rugged watch. For everyday use, the Series 12 offers better value; if you already own an Ultra 3, compare the cost of upgrading with how much its extra eight hours of rated battery life and new health features matter to you. Should I buy an older Apple Watch? Foundry The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are now the previous-generation models and may be good buys if retailers discount them enough. Before choosing any older Apple Watch, check both its price against the current model and whether it can run watchOS 27. The Series 9 and Ultra 2 are the oldest supported Apple Watch models models in their respective ranges; the SE 3 is the only supported SE. The following models cannot install watchOS 27, so we would generally avoid buying them unless the price is exceptionally low and you are comfortable using older software: Apple Watch Series 6 (2020) Apple Watch Series 7 (2021) Apple Watch Series 8 (2022) Apple Watch SE (2nd generation, 2022) Apple Watch Ultra (1st generation, 2022) Start by comparing a discounted Series 11 with the Series 12, or an Ultra 3 with the Ultra 4. The Series 11 retains the Series 12’s 24-hour everyday battery rating but lacks its new Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features. The Ultra 3 retains satellite communication and dual-frequency GPS, but its rated battery life is 42 hours rather than the Ultra 4’s 50 hours. Series 10 and Ultra 2 can offer further savings if their price and battery condition make sense; Series 9 is the oldest standard model that runs watchOS 27. What to look for when buying an older Apple Watch Choose an S9 chip or newer for the longest software support. Buy refurbished if possible. Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store includes a one-year warranty, while reputable third-party refurbishers can also offer good value. Shop during major sales. Previous-generation Apple Watches often receive their biggest discounts during Prime Day and Black Friday. Check the battery and Activation Lock. If you’re buying used, confirm the battery is in good condition, inspect the watch for damage, and make sure Activation Lock has been removed before you buy. Model Key advantage When it’s a good buy Apple Watch Series 11 Recent standard watch with 24-hour rated battery life. When discounted enough that you’re happy to give up the Series 12’s new health sensing and upcoming Audio Intelligence features. Apple Watch Ultra 3 Ultra outdoor features, including satellite communication. When substantially cheaper than Ultra 4 and its 42-hour rated battery life is enough for you. Apple Watch Series 10 A further saving on a standard Apple Watch. When notably cheaper than Series 11 and in good condition. Apple Watch Ultra 2 Rugged watch that supports watchOS 27. When notably cheaper than Ultra 3 and its older battery and connectivity specifications meet your needs. Apple Watch Series 9 Oldest standard model compatible with watchOS 27. Only when the saving is substantial and its battery is in good condition. Apple Watch Series 11 (42mm) Read our review Price When Reviewed: $399 Best Prices Today: $364.99 at Best Buy US | $399 at Amazon | $399 at Walmart Apple Watch Ultra 3 Read our review Price When Reviewed: $799 Best Prices Today: $799 at Amazon | $799 at Best Buy US Apple Watch Series 10 (42mm) Read our review Price When Reviewed: $399 Best Prices Today: $274 at Walmart | $329 at Best Buy | $370 at Best Buy US Apple Watch Ultra 2 Read our review Price When Reviewed: $799 (base) Best Prices Today: $599.95 at Best Buy US | $799 at Apple | $799.99 at Target When is the best time to buy an Apple Watch? The best time to buy an Apple Watch depends on whether you want the newest model or the lowest price. The Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now on sale, alongside the SE 3. If you want the latest model and are happy with its price, you can buy now without an imminent replacement to worry about. If getting a discount matters more, compare retailers during the expected October sales and Black Friday in November. The September launch also makes the Series 11 and Ultra 3 worth checking. Retailers may reduce remaining stock, but compare the actual saving with the features you would give up: the Series 12 and Ultra 4 add new health sensing, while the Ultra 4 also increases rated battery life from 42 to 50 hours. Apple kept the new models’ starting prices at $399/£369 for Series 12 and $799/£749 for Ultra 4. Individual configurations and retailer prices vary. When shouldn’t you buy an Apple Watch? Avoid buying an Apple Watch: Just before Apple’s annual September event, unless you need one immediately. At full price when a major sale is only days away, such as Prime Day or Black Friday. Without comparing prices. Check multiple retailers and use price-tracking tools such as CamelCamelCamel to avoid inflated “sale” prices. If you’re paying extra for cellular but don’t need it . Cellular Apple Watch typically cost around $100 more and require a monthly data plan, while the GPS model offers better value for most people. If battery life is your top priority. Apple Watch battery life still trails some competing smartwatches, so you may prefer an alternative platform if multi-day battery life is essential. Best time to buy Why Prime Day (July/October) Best deals on current-generation models. Black Friday (November) Consistently some of the lowest prices of the year. After the September launch Previous-generation models receive substantial discounts. Worst time: August to early September New Apple Watches are expected within weeks. U.S. deals Apple Watch Deal MSRP Lowest Apple Watch Series 11, 42mm, GPS $299 Get the deal at Amazon $100 off $399 $279 Apple Watch Series 11, 46mm, GPS $329 Get the deal at Amazon $100 off $429 $309 Apple Watch Ultra 3 $779 Get the deal at Amazon $30 off $799 $649 Apple Watch SE 3, 40mm, GPS $219 Get the deal at Amazon $30 off $249 $199 Apple Watch SE 3, 44mm, GPS $249 Get the deal at Amazon $30 off $279 $229 U.K. deals Apple Watch Deal RRP Lowest Apple Watch Series 11, 42mm, GPS £299 Get the deal at Amazon £70 off £369 £287 Apple Watch Series 11, 46mm, GPS £319 Get the deal at Amazon £80 off £399 £317 Apple Watch Ultra 3 £729 Get the deal at Amazon £20 off £749 £649 Apple Watch SE 3, 40mm, GPS £219 at Amazon £219 £197 Apple Watch SE 3, 44mm, GPS £219 Get the deal at Amazon £30 off £249 £189.05 Where to find the best Apple Watch deals IDG Apple rarely discounts the Apple Watch itself, so the best deals are usually found at third-party retailers – we check these every month and record the best deals here: Top Apple Watch discounts & deals – Big savings on all models . Best places to buy : Amazon is consistently one of the best places to find Apple Watch discounts, particularly during major sales. Other good options in the U.S. include Best Buy , Walmart , Target and Costco . In the U.K., check Amazon , Currys , Argos , John Lewis and KRCS . Shop during major sales : The biggest discounts typically arrive during Amazon Prime Day (July and October) and Black Friday/Cyber Monday (November). Savings of $100–$150 on current-generation models are common. During Prime Day 2026, for example, the Apple Watch Series 11 fell to $279 ($120 off) and the Ultra 3 dropped to $649 ($150 off). Check for education discounts : Students, teachers and education staff may qualify for discounted Apple Watch pricing through Apple’s Education Store U.S. (and Education Store U.K. ). For more information read our guide to how to get a student discount at the Apple Education Store . Tip : Before buying, compare prices across several retailers and check the recent price history with a tool such as CamelCamelCamel to make sure you’re getting a genuine deal rather than a temporary “discount” from an inflated price. Is it worth buying a refurbished Apple Watch? Buying a refurbished Apple Watch is another great way to save money, provided you buy from a reputable seller and choose a model that will continue to receive software updates. Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store is the safest option. Every watch undergoes rigorous testing, cleaning and inspection, comes with a one-year warranty, includes new accessories, and is eligible for AppleCare. Apart from the plain white box, it’s difficult to tell the difference between a refurbished Apple Watch and a brand-new one. You can typically save around 15% on recent models, with even bigger discounts on older generations. Check Apple’s U.S. Refurbished Store or U.K. Refurbished Store for current models, configurations and prices. Stock changes regularly; compare any refurbished Series 11 or Ultra 3 with the price of a new Series 12 or Ultra 4 before buying. The best Apple Watch refurbished deals: Apple’s U.S. Refurbished Store often has Apple Watch Series 11, 10 and 9, SE 3, SE 2, Ultra 2 and Ultra 3. Get a refurbished Apple Watch Series 11 for $339, $60 off You may also find the Apple Watch Series 11, 10 and 9, SE 2, SE 3 and Ultra 3 at Apple’s U.K. Refurbished Store . Get a refurbished Apple Watch Series 11 for £309, £60 off Third-party refurbishers can also offer excellent value, but quality varies. Terms such as “Excellent” or “Grade A”aren’t standardised, so always check the seller’s warranty, return policy and battery condition before buying. Be aware that Amazon Renewed devices, for example, aren’t refurbished to Apple’s standards and may not include a new battery or replacement parts. The other key consideration is software support. Older Apple Watches eventually stop receiving new versions of watchOS, so avoid buying a model that’s nearing the end of its supported life. For the best balance of price and features, compare refurbished Series 11 and Ultra 3 models with the new generation first. Series 9, Series 10 and Ultra 2 can cost less and still run watchOS 27, but check their condition and savings carefully. A refurbished Apple Watch can be one of the best values in Apple’s lineup – as long as you buy from a trusted seller and don’t choose a model that’s too old. Read: Should I buy a refurbished Apple Watch? for more information. FAQ 1. Should I wait for the next Apple Watch? You do not need to wait for 2026’s launch: the Series 12 and Ultra 4 went on sale in September 2026, and the SE 3 remains in Apple’s lineup. If you need a watch now, choose the model that fits your needs and budget. If you are mainly looking for a lower price, consider waiting for a sale or comparing discounted Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock. Apple has not announced when the next Apple Watch models will arrive, but we expect that the next update will happen in September 2027. 2. How long does Apple support an Apple Watch? Apple has traditionally supported Apple Watches with major watchOS updates for around five to six years, but that changed with watchOS 27, announced at WWDC 2026. Apple dropped support for five older models in a single release: Apple Watch Series 6 (2020) Apple Watch Series 7 (2021) Apple Watch Series 8 (2022) Apple Watch SE (2nd generation, 2022) Apple Watch Ultra (1st generation, 2022) As a result, watchOS 27 only supports Apple Watches with an S9 chip or later, starting with the Apple Watch Series 9. While Apple may continue to provide security updates for older models for a limited time, they no longer receive new watchOS features. The change makes software support a much more important consideration when buying an older or refurbished Apple Watch. If you want the longest possible lifespan, choose a model with an S9 chip or newer. 3. Is the Apple Watch Series 11 still worth buying? If it is substantially cheaper than the Series 12. Both have up to 24 hours of rated everyday battery life, but the Series 12 adds more frequent heart-rate and HRV measurements, a Readiness score and support for upcoming Audio Intelligence features, so be sure that you are willing to give those features up for the saving.

sections.body: While PC component prices remain high, you can save a good bit of money on a system by purchasing a prebuilt desktop. Walmart has a well-equipped CyberPowerPC gaming PC on sale for $1,549, almost $600 off its original price of $2,139. It’s powered by an Intel Core i7-14700KF processor, and paired with 32GB of 6000MHz DDR5 memory and an Nvidia RTX 5070 Founders Edition with 12GB of VRAM. The case is a CyberPowerPC MA-O1 , an in-house design with extensive cooling options and three dedicated knobs for adjusting internal RGB lighting colors.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: While it might not feel like it at first blush, this is a solid value for a gaming PC that’s ready to rock out of the box. The RTX 5070 in this machine is likely to run you upwards of $800 by itself at the moment ( it launched in 2025 for $549 ), and 32GB of fast memory can be $400 or more. For just a small premium, you get those components packed into a nice case with a panoramic glass panel and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD inside. The whole kit is tested, with a one year warranty for parts and labor. It also includes a keyboard and mouse, so you can start gaming right away once it arrives.

article.title: iPhone 18 Pro review: The best kind of boring
article.summary: It’s hard to get excited about a new iPhone that is just “the same thing but faster and with a slightly better camera,” especially when the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time. But the impressive A20 Pro performance and efficiency really help make this the iPhone Pro to beat all others.

draft_context.description: Macworld At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Crazy-fast performance Better cooling performance A “pro” camera that finally feels like it Cons The price went up There are no major new features The design is the same Our Verdict It’s hard to get excited about a new iPhone that is just “the same thing but faster and with a slightly better camera,” especially when the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time. But the impressive A20 Pro performance and efficiency really help make this the iPhone Pro to beat all others. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today The iPhone 18 Pro is just like last year’s iPhone, but faster and with a slightly better camera. That’s it. Back in the early iPhone days, we would call this an “S” model, because a year after the iPhone 4, there was the iPhone 4s . A year after the iPhone 5, the 5s . After the 6, the 6s . And each one was physically identical to its predecessor, but faster and with a somewhat better camera. If you wanted to think of this as the iPhone 17 Pro S, you’d be spot on. The thing about those “S” models is that, while they were kind of boring, they were still the best iPhones. So is it with this year’s model—there’s no incredible new feature or design change to get excited about, but that “same but better” formula results in one of the best iPhones in a long time. The iPhone 17 Pro, but better Last year, Apple introduced a new Cosmic Orange color for iPhone 17 Pro that shocked everyone with its boldness. It was an instant hit. So it’s a little disappointing that the only thing visually different about the iPhone 18 Pro is that they got rid of Cosmic Orange and replaced it with Burgundy. Which is a fine color, but it’s no Cosmic Orange. There’s a black and a silver this year, along with a new pale blue called Glacier . The iPhone 18 Pro, show in Glacier blue, is much more subdued than the ultra-bright 17 Pro Foundry Beyond the colors, you’d be hard-pressed to notice a difference between last year’s pro iPhones and this year’s. They have the same dimensions, though this year’s phones are just a touch heavier. They’re so similar that some cases for the iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max will fit the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max just fine. Certain other cases fit poorly because the camera plateau is about a half-millimeter taller on the new phones; it all depends on the design of the case. You’ll also notice, when the iPhone is on, that the Dynamic Island cutout is just a little smaller, which leaves enough room for two dynamic activities to be tracked at once. Apple moved the IR sensor used with Face ID under the display and off to the side, behind a row of pixels with some sub-pixels removed and others made brighter to compensate. You can’t see it at all, and in my testing it seems to work just fine. But I also haven’t really found the smaller Dynamic Island has changed things much for me, either. It’s what’s on the inside that makes the 18 Pro special: a new processor system and some camera improvements. iPhone 18 Pro: A20 Pro performance The A20 Pro is Apple’s first chip built on a 2nm process, and it’s seriously impressive. It’s not just the chip itself that makes the difference here; it’s what we might call the A20 Pro system . It involves a new packaging technique that puts the RAM off to the side of the chip for better cooling and an all new vapor chamber…also for better cooling. It’s still a six-core CPU, but both the “Super” cores and the efficiency cores are improved, and the memory bus is 50 percent wider, providing 50 percent more bandwidth. The GPU is 7 cores, up for 6 in the A19 Pro, and also features architectural improvements. Take a look at these numbers. Foundry In the older Geekbench 6 test, single-core performance jumps an impressive 26 percent. The multi-core score is up even more at 30 percent higher. That’s a crazy jump for one year. Foundry The more modern Geekbench 7 tests are also more strenuous, but the results are the same: a single-core score is 26 percent higher and a multi-core score is 28 percent higher. Apple calls its big cores “desktop class” and that’s not just hype. This is single-core performance that is higher than an M5 and multi-core performance equal to an M3. In your phone . In your pocket . To put this CPU performance in context, this is a single-core score that beats the best Ryzen or Intel Core i7 desktop CPUs without exotic overclocking, and a multi-core score in the same range as most 8-core desktop CPUs from two or three years ago. As impressive as the CPU is, the GPU seems to get an even bigger speed boost. Let’s take a lot at GPU performance for computational tasks (image segmentation, horizon detection, blurring backgrounds, face detection, and so on) using Geekbench 7’s GPU test. Foundry A 46 percent jump in GPU compute performance in a single year? It seems unthinkable, but Apple increased memory bandwidth by 50 percent and that is often a bottleneck for all kinds of graphics performance. For context, an M4 Mac scores around 54,000 in this test—13 percent slower. This is performance somewhere in-between the M1 Pro and the regular M5. In your pocket. But that’s GPU compute. Surely when it comes to rendering complex 3D graphics like the kind used for high-end games, and stressing the CPU at the same time, the improvement isn’t as big? Think again. Foundry Through several generations of 3DMark real-time graphics benchmarks, we see massive improvements with the A20 Pro. The relatively simple Wild Life Extreme test is 93 percent faster, almost twice as fast! The Solar Bay benchmark stepped up complexity and added some ray tracing elements, and the A20 Pro is 57 percent faster that last year’s A19 Pro. Steel Nomad Light is the heaviest test, though it doesn’t feature any ray tracing. It’s 53 percent faster. This is graphics rendering performance that is faster than the M4 an an iPad Pro and almost as fast as an M5. Spot-checking with actual games, which are harder to benchmark in a deterministic fashion, we see a lot of the same results. Most games either just lock at 60 frames per second, or they’re anywhere from 40 percent faster to almost twice as fast. The Neural Engine is more difficult to test, but the Geekbench AI benchmark affords us the ability to get a look at running machine learning routines on the Neural Engine alone if we want. Foundry Most of the ML/AI code that runs on neural processing units (NPUs) are the lighter half-precision and quantized routines that demand quick results in a power-efficient way. The new Neural Engine has double the cores and runs these sorts of tasks more than 40 percent faster. Apple’s been steadily improving Neural Engine performance for years, but we usually see a 20-30 percent boost, not this. Again, this is desktop-class stuff. An M5 doesn’t deliver scores like this, even. Apple doubled the Neural Engine cores in the M6, though, and that manages to pull ahead of the A20 Pro. I’ve been testing and reviewing consumer tech for over 20 years, from early DIY gaming PCs through mobile technology and beyond. I’m not easily impressed by a year-over-year performance improvement. But the A20 Pro has me genuinely shocked. Single-core, multi-core, GPU, Neural Engine…it’s all drastically faster than the A19 Pro, which was already at the top of its class. In test after test, the A20 Pro delivers results that equal desktop-class chips of the sort you’d find in thin-and-light laptops bought in the last year or two. iPhone 18 Pro: Camera improvements For all the “pro” features Apple has added to the Pro iPhone cameras over the years — ProRAW photos, ProRES video, Dolby Vision, Genlock syncing, and so on — the actual photo-taking experience has felt decidedly point-and-shoot. If you wanted to take real control over your shots, you’d have to ditch the default Camera app and use a third-party app such as Halide or Blackmagic Camera . This year, Apple has finally added what it calls “Pro controls” to the Camera app, which eliminates the need to use one of those apps for most photographers that want more than point-and-shoot style control. You get menus to adjust white balance, focus distance, shutter speed, and lens aperture, and can display a real-time histogram. Foundry It’s hard to believe that it took Apple this long to provide these basic manual controls, at least for the “Pro” iPhones. And it should be a scandal that they’re only available on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, instead of coming as a software update to earlier Pro models. There’s nothing about any of these controls, save for the aperture setting, that need to be exclusive to this year’s models. And indeed, most of them are alredy available on third-party apps. About that aperture setting. It’s true, the main camera (and only the main camera) now has an adjustable physical aperture. It only has four settings: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. It defaults to f/1.8, which is a similar aperture wideness to earlier iPhones, and performs about the same. But it’s neat to see it move! Foundry The f/1.48 is wider and lets in more light, so it kicks in during low-light scenes, but an aperture that wide on a sensor this small results in slightly less sharp photos. So it wouldn’t be a good setting for a fixed-aperture lens on other iPhones, but it’s nice to have in a pinch. Moving up to higher f-stop numbers makes the aperture smaller, which lets in less light and is more appropriate for bright daytime photography. It also makes the focus depth longer, so more of the background is in focus. Foundry Here’s an example. Focusing on the tree in the foreground, you can see the ladder in the background get a bit sharper as the aperture gets smaller. The effect is not dramatic; small sensors are less responsive to this sort of thing, and a maximum F-stop of 4 is still pretty wide. Most full-frame cameras have a maximum F-stop of at least F/16 or F/22. Users have complained for years now that Apple’s more recent image processing pipelines tend to make photos look worse than they did on older phones. The chief complaint seems to be oversaturation of colors and tone and a “plastic” effect that loses all grain and texture. This year, Apple has tweaked its Photographic Styles setup yet again to give users more control over color temperature and tone. New this year is a “texture” setting that lets you increase or decrease fine texture detail or adjust the amount of skin smoothing or brightening. Foundry It’s another good attempt to bring some authenticity and humanity back into photos that, by their very nature, are very processed. I like it, but I think Apple may have been better off paying attention to the “ Process Zero ” fad sweeping the third-party camera apps lately, and provided a similar control of its own. Just a one-button, “minimal processing” setting that turns off all the AI help and gives you an authentic image, warts and all. There a couple of other new tricks. A smart focus tracking feature lets you tap on an object and the focus will follow it as it moves. And Apple Reference Image, which signs individual pixels of the image and makes the original available all the time, to verify it has not been edited. You have to turn that on in Settings > Camera > Apple Reference Image , and then you have to take photos using the new Reference mode that appears. I suspect it won’t be used much outside of photojournalism. Apple’s big advancement this year, the variable aperture camera, is a bit of a letdown. There’s just not enough aperture range for it to make a big difference with this small sensor. The new software controls, on the other hand, are very welcome and most of them should have been included on the Pro phones years ago. As much as I appreciate their inclusion in the standard Camera app today, I find it frustrating that Apple limits them to the iPhone 18 Pro for no good reason. iPhone 18 Pro: Battery, charging, and thermal improvements The A20 Pro’s performance is off-the-charts good, but it doesn’t suffer from poor efficiency at all. Quite the opposite. I used Geekbench 4’s battery benchmark, which runs sporadic tests in the background to keep the processor busy. It’s a more realistic and repeatable test than a typical video playback benchmark. (Dear Primate Labs : Please incorporate a new battery test in Geekbench 7!) I kept the display fixed at 200 nits of brightness, which is about midway on the brightness slider, and turned off all dynamic brightness and low-battery mode features. Foundry We’re looking at a 12 percent increase in battery life from last year’s model. The iPhone 18 Pro Max, which is identical in every way except size and battery, lasts an impressive 25 percent longer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. It really is impressive to see how far iPhone battery life has come in just a few years. In three generations, Apple has more than doubled the real usable battery life of the iPhone Pro models. It has sort of flown under the radar, but Apple improved charging speed this year as well. Foundry The iPhone 18 Pro charges at a little bit higher rate from 0-80 percent, then sort of flatlines at around 10W or less for the rest of the charge curve. This gets it to 50 percent a few mintues faster than the iPhone 17 Pro, to 80 percent about 10 minutes faster, and to 100 percent almost 20 minutes faster. It’s not a huge improvement, and it’s not as fast as the very fastest-charging Android phones, but it’s a noticeable improvement all the same. Apple has made a big deal out of its new thermal solution, with a much bigger vapor chamber and a new chip packaging technique that moves the RAM to the side so it and the processor can be cooled more effectively. It’s a difficult thing to reliably test, but I can say from a year of experience with the iPhone 17 Pro that the iPhone 18 Pro definitely gets less hot. Playing certain games, recording extended video, and other long-term intensive tasks would often make the iPhone 17 Pro rather hot to the touch. I can’t claim that the 18 Pro stays cool in these same situations, but the heat buildup is very obviously less. Should you buy an iPhone 18 Pro? The iPhone 18 Pro could truly be called the iPhone 17 Pro S. It looks and acts the same as last year’s flagship. The only really new features are a variable aperture feature that doesn’t really make that much of a difference and some really welcome Camera app upgrades that have been available in third-party apps for years, and have no real business being locked to the new phone. The A20 Pro is a revelation. It’s a high high water mark for mobile performance and efficiency, with real speeds that push into laptop territory and even longer battery life than the very good battery life of last year’s iPhone. It’s a year-over-year performance leap we almost never see anymore. But it doesn’t enable anything new . The phone looks the same, and most of the features are the same. There’s no special AI thing or awesome new capability you get with the iPhone 18 Pro that you don’t get with the iPhone 17 Pro (outside of the variable aperture and aforementioned photography features that other apps have). So this year’s best iPhone is last year’s best iPhone, only more so. Much faster. Longer battery life. Faster charging. And a camera that’s just a bit better. Oh, and the price went up by $100, or $300 if you get the highest storage tiers. iPhone 17 Pro S indeed.

draft_context.source_title: The Download: India’s smart glasses menace and AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
draft_context.description: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes. Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive. The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance. Here’s why smart glasses are creating new privacy risks in India . —Anuj Behal MIT Technology Review Narrated: what’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble When Jessica Wachter, a University of Pennsylvania finance professor, wanted to assess AI’s impact on the economy over the next few years, she started with a simple fact: a handful of so-called hyperscalers are investing huge amounts of money to build AI data centers. Instead of trying to predict how widely deployed AI models will be, Wachter asked how fast the hyperscalers’ earnings will need to grow to justify their spending through 2027, when expenditures are expected to reach nearly $1.1 trillion. The results are eye-opening. AI companies will need to achieve an extraordinary increase in productivity just to break even by 2030 . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Hackers claim they’ve stolen data on almost all FBI employees The ShinyHunters group says it seized more than 2 TB of data. ( Axios ) + Including agents’ names, addresses, and phone numbers. ( 404 Media ) + ShinyHunters says the attack was retaliation for an FBI alert. ( Reuters $) + Now is a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Anthropic and OpenAI have both released lower-cost models They face growing competition from cheaper Chinese models. ( CNBC ) + Startups have been reducing their reliance on the two labs. ( Bloomberg $) + The new models are the first since their calls for an AI slowdown. ( FT $) + Their CEOs are set to brief the UN Security Council today. ( Quartz ) + Could AI really kill us all? ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Trump’s Treasury chief could soon become his new AI czar Scott Bessent has played a central role in US-China AI talks. ( Semafor ) + Other contenders include Michael Kratsios and Scott Kupor. ( Gizmodo ) + Will Trump’s AI rebrand to “superintelligence” catch on? ( BBC ) 4 Scientists are turning renewable electricity directly into food The goal is to make more food with less land. ( New Scientist $) + Companies are creating food out of thin air. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 A “fire amoeba” has broken the heat survival record for complex life The newly discovered organism can grow and reproduce at 63°C. ( NPR ) + It could inform the search for life elsewhere. ( New Scientist $) 6 Meta quietly tested a “human concierge” for its Muse AI agent Contractors secretly handled some calls placed by Muse. ( Reuters $) + Staff raised concerns about privacy and misleading users. ( 404 Media ) 7 Data centres are replacing copper with light to cut energy use Photonics can move data with less heat than electrical wiring. ( BBC ) + Virtual power plants could also help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 AI models built from rat brains just got closer to reality AWS is tapping rat neurons to make video AI faster. ( Wired $) 9 Uber is betting on human drivers to give its robotaxis an edge They can cover demand spikes while autonomous cars recharge. ( Axios ) 10 A humanoid robot took on an amateur fighter in a cage The brief bout was billed as the first human-robot MMA fight. ( Futurism ) Quote of the day “The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake. It’s not fake; it’s actually amazing.” —President Donald Trump tells the UN General Assembly why he wants to rename AI “superintelligence.” One more thing COURTESY OF PAINCHEK AI is changing how we quantify pain At Orchard Care Homes, nurses used to rely on an observational scale to assess pain in residents who couldn’t communicate verbally. But agitated residents were sometimes assumed to have behavioral issues, while their pain went untreated. Then, in 2021, the care-home chain began trialing PainChek, a smartphone app that scans a resident’s face for microscopic muscle movements and uses AI to output a pain score. Within weeks, the pilot unit saw fewer prescriptions and calmer corridors. Now researchers are racing to turn pain into something a camera or sensor can score as reliably as blood pressure. When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes.

Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.
The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance.

sections.body: For the past eight hours I had been in the basement of a dorm in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, playing a board game called Diplomacy along with six other men. Each of us was vying against 80 other people to be crowned the world champion of Diplomacy at the end of the weekend here at Dixiecon. 1 One of those men, Brian Ecton, a high school math teacher from Prince George’s County, Maryland, with hair like Katt Williams and a mouth to match, approached me right at the start, sizing me up as a beginner and offering an alliance. He explained exactly how it would work and said we’d share a draw at the end. I had no reason not to agree.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: For the next several hours each of the other players would take turns dragging me aside to explain to me how Brian was manipulating me, how he was going to betray me, how I should betray him first and work with them against Brian. I dismissed them all. After all, who’s to say they wouldn’t betray me as well? I was outmatched in this game. Safer to pick a player and stick with him come what may, I thought. But here I stood, on the verge of elimination, and the other players were pissed. According to them, I could have avoided this if I had listened to them hours ago.

article.summary: HONOR chọn thời điểm này để phát hành đoạn phim ngắn mang tên "Bờ Tây của biển" (nguyên gốc tiếng Trung: 海的两端), do diễn viên Vương Ngạn Đồng đóng chính. Phim kể về một người con xa quê cầm bút viết thư bằng tiếng Triều Châu gửi về cho bà, giữa lúc trăng rằm sắp tròn.

Toàn bộ đoạn phim được quay bằng HONOR Magic9 Pro Max, mẫu điện thoại cao cấp sắp ra mắt của HONOR.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Điểm khiến đoạn phim này gây chú ý không nằm ở kỹ xảo hay bối cảnh, mà ở việc HONOR chọn đúng Vương Ngạn Đồng cho vai diễn. Nam diễn viên sinh năm 1999 tại Sán Đầu, Quảng Đông, không xuất thân khoa bảng diễn xuất, từng nổi lên nhờ vai Trịnh Mộc Sinh trong phim điện ảnh "Thư Tình Gửi Bà" (tên tiếng Anh: Dear You) của đạo diễn Lam Hồng Xuân. Phim nói chủ yếu bằng tiếng Triều Châu, dàn diễn viên phần lớn không chuyên, kể chuyện qua "kiều phê" - những lá thư người Hoa kiều gửi về quê từ nhiều thập kỷ trước. Ra rạp từ suất chiếu ngày đầu chỉ 1,6% phòng chiếu, phim sau đó vươn lên vị trí thứ 2 phòng vé Trung Quốc năm 2026 với hơn 18,6 tỷ tệ (khoảng 71.000 tỷ đồng), đạt điểm 9,0-9,2 trên Douban - một trong 4 phim điện ảnh nội địa Trung Quốc vượt mốc 9 điểm trong gần 10 năm qua.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Chính vì vậy, đoạn phim Trung Thu của HONOR gần như là phần nối dài đời thực của nhân vật Trịnh Mộc Sinh, không phải một kịch bản quảng cáo thông thường. Khoảnh khắc Vương Ngạn Đồng cầm lá thư lên, ánh sáng hoài cổ và giọng Triều Châu quen thuộc khiến người xem liên tưởng ngay đến nhân vật từng khiến khán giả khóc ngoài rạp hồi tháng 5. HONOR không thuê một gương mặt đóng vai người xa quê, mà mượn chính biểu tượng văn hóa "xa quê" đang được cả Trung Quốc yêu thích để kể lại đúng câu chuyện đó, đúng dịp đoàn viên.

draft_context.source_title: Tỷ phú AI Alexandr Wang gây sốt với chiếc áo 'giàu ngầm'
draft_context.description: Áo phông lạ mắt của Alexandr Wang, Giám đốc AI của Meta, được cho là áo Hermès trị giá 800 USD.
paragraphs: Tại hội nghị thường niên dành cho nhà phát triển Connect 2026 của Meta hôm 23/9, Alexandr Wang mặc áo phông in hình theo phong cách những năm 1990: phía trên là đầu hươu lớn, bên dưới là con đường mòn trong rừng cùng những con hươu nhỏ, tay áo in dòng chữ "Lake Tahoe". Ông phối áo với quần tối màu và dép Crocs rằn ri.

Sau khi bài phát biểu của Wang tại Connect 2026 được chia sẻ, nhiều người dùng mạng xã hội lập tức chú ý đến trang phục của ông. Một số cho rằng đây là phong cách "giàu ngầm" (quiet luxury), và bộ đồ thực chất rất đắt.

Tài khoản Goltra trên X phân tích từng món đồ, cho rằng Wang mặc áo Hermès giá 800 USD, quần Loro Piana giá 1.200 USD và dép Ferragamo giá 1.500 USD. Bài đăng thu hút 3,4 triệu lượt xem cùng hàng trăm bình luận sau một ngày. Tài khoản gazar47 đăng lại hình ảnh này kèm ghi chú: "Tôi đánh giá rất tích cực về Wang, trông có vẻ anh ấy đã tập gym".

Tuy nhiên, Wang nhanh chóng phủ nhận việc mình mặc đồ xa xỉ, gọi đây là "vu khống". Ông cho biết, mình mua áo trong cửa hàng đồ cũ tại Santa Cruz với giá 30 USD, quần giá 150 USD và dép Crocs khoảng 60 USD. Phản hồi bài đăng của gazar47 , Wang hài hước viết: "Thật ra, nếu bạn nói tôi trông cân đối thì tôi chẳng quan tâm bạn nói dối về giá quần áo đến mức nào đâu".

Business Insider nhận xét, trang phục của Wang khớp với cách ông quảng bá cho trợ lý AI Muse của Meta trên mạng: ít mang vẻ tương lai bóng bẩy của một tập đoàn, mà đậm chất hỗn loạn, ngẫu hứng của một nhà sáng lập tích cực hoạt động online.

Đây không phải lần đầu Wang mặc áo phông hình hươu. Giám đốc AI Meta từng mặc áo này trong chương trình podcast Core Memory hồi tháng 5 và cho một số cuộc họp nội bộ lớn. Business Insider phỏng đoán đây có thể là áo phông vintage thập niên 1990 hiệu "Back to Earth". Có một số mẫu áo của thương hiệu này trên nền tảng thương mại điện tử eBay và Poshmark khá giống với giá khoảng 14-45 USD.

draft_context.source_title: Spotlight on SIG Apps
draft_context.description: As Kubernetes adoption has grown, the conversation has shifted beyond running containers to managing increasingly complex application lifecycles. Modern platforms support stateless web services, stateful databases, batch processing, AI workloads, and platform services. At the same time, they must remain reliable during upgrades, scaling events, and infrastructure failures. Every Kubernetes user relies on SIG Apps, whether they realize it or not. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs form the foundation of how applications are deployed, updated, scaled, and operated across the Kubernetes ecosystem. SIG Apps is focused on improving workload resilience, refining application lifecycle management, and addressing the operational challenges that emerge when applications encounter node failures, rollout disruptions, and increasingly complex infrastructure environments. In this spotlight, we sit down with two of the three SIG Apps chairs Janet Kuo and Maciej Szulik to discuss the evolution of Kubernetes workload management, the challenges of balancing application reliability with operational simplicity, and the future of application lifecycle management within one of Kubernetes’ most influential Special Interest Groups. Introducing SIG Apps Natalie Fisher: Can you introduce yourself, your role, and how you got involved in SIG Apps? Janet Kuo: I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. In those early days, my focus was on building the core Workloads API, specifically developing controllers like Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, and DaemonSet, defining their rollout behaviors, and bringing them from initial designs to GA. That hands-on work was my entry point into SIG Apps. Since then, I've stayed deeply involved in both the technical and community sides of Kubernetes. I have led SIG Apps as Co-Chair and Tech Lead since 2019. Currently, in addition to maintaining the workloads API, I am driving new subprojects like the Agent Sandbox to ensure Kubernetes is ready for next-generation agentic and AI workloads. Maciej Szulik: I started contributing to Kubernetes all the way back in 2014 . Since then, I've worked across various areas of the project: controllers, kubectl, and apimachinery, which eventually led me to become one of the Chairs and Tech Leads for SIG Apps. My current focus is reliability of the workload controllers under the SIG Apps umbrella and stability and ease of use of kubectl as part of my SIG CLI Tech Lead role. I also care about overall community health and growth as part of my Steering Committee role. Outside of Kubernetes, I work as a Staff Platform Engineer at Defense Unicorns, where I'm helping make Kubernetes more airgap-native with a project called zarf . The problem and the solution SIG Apps is responsible for the core workload APIs that power how applications run on Kubernetes. From Deployments and StatefulSets to Jobs and CronJobs, these controllers determine how workloads are created, updated, scaled, and recovered when things go wrong. As Kubernetes expands to support increasingly diverse workloads – including AI, batch processing, and large-scale distributed applications – SIG Apps continues to evolve these APIs while balancing reliability, backward compatibility, and operational simplicity. NF: For readers who may not be familiar, what is SIG Apps, and what role does it play within the broader Kubernetes ecosystem? MS: SIG Apps is the Kubernetes Special Interest Group responsible for the workloads APIs. CronJob and Job help running batch workloads, whereas DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, and StatefulSet serve the majority of other applications. More broadly, SIG Apps owns the layer most developers actually touch day-to-day: the controllers that turn a workload specification into running, self-healing pods. It's the group deciding how Deployments roll out, how Jobs retry, how DaemonSets place a pod per node. JK: Adding to what Maciej described, as the industry shifts, we are seeing a massive demand to run complex, non-traditional workloads like distributed AI training, batch computing, and dynamic agent environments. Our role is expanding: we aren't just maintaining the classic workloads API, but we are actively evolving it and establishing new patterns (like the Agent Sandbox ) to make sure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. NF: Looking at the workload APIs owned by SIG Apps (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs), which areas are receiving the most attention from maintainers and contributors? MS: After a long stretch focused on making batch workloads run smoothly on Kubernetes, we’ve shifted attention to make sure serving workloads (DaemonSets, StatefulSets, etc) aren’t left behind. This means performance and high-scale improvements to rollout and scaling behavior, plus working through our backlog of user-reported issues, prioritizing the ones with the strongest support from the user base. Current focus areas As Kubernetes workloads grow in scale and complexity, the challenges facing workload controllers evolve as well. We asked the SIG Apps chairs where contributors are focusing their efforts today and which resilience problems they believe are the highest priorities. NF: From your perspective, what are the most important workload resilience problems SIG Apps is trying to solve today? MS: Node lifecycle challenges have come up repeatedly across SIG Apps, SIG Node, and SIG Autoscaling discussions. DaemonSets and Jobs are just where the pain is most visible, since they're the workloads most directly bound to node state. Rather than solve it piecemeal within one SIG, we've settled on spinning up a dedicated Node Lifecycle Working Group to focus on this properly and hopefully land long-term solutions instead of one-off patches. JK: From an AI perspective, resilience is critical. When you are running a massive distributed LLM training job that spans hundreds of GPUs, a single node failure can halt the entire pipeline. Similarly, if a DaemonSet that runs your logging or GPU monitoring agent gets stuck on a bad node, it impacts the entire cluster's health. In addition to the work in the Node Lifecycle WG to handle infrastructure-level degradation, SIG Apps is addressing this at the orchestration layer through subprojects like JobSet (for distributed training) and LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) (for sharded LLM inference). These APIs introduce patterns like "all-or-nothing" failure handling, where a single pod or job failure triggers a coordinated group-level restart to resume from the last clean checkpoint, rather than letting stuck workloads hang in an inconsistent state. Real-world impact The work happening within SIG Apps extends far beyond controller implementations and API design. We wanted to understand what these improvements mean in practice for platform teams operating Kubernetes clusters in production. NF: For platform teams operating Kubernetes in production, what practical improvements would they notice if the node lifecycle and workload resilience work currently under discussion is successfully delivered? MS: I’m mostly looking from the sidelines, the folks actually in the Node Lifecycle Working Group would give you a sharper answer. But from where I sit, I’m hoping their work translates into fewer 3am pages that turn out to be “a DaemonSet rollout got stuck because node X was flaky, and someone had to manually cordon/delete/restart to unstick it.” JK: +1 to what Maciej said, and beyond reducing manual intervention, platform teams will also see much better resource predictability and cost efficiency. For example, in AI workloads where GPU idle time is extremely expensive, having Kubernetes automatically detect a degraded node and reschedule the training coordinator or agent before the job crashes means less wasted compute and more stable job execution. Challenges and trade-offs Evolving APIs that millions of workloads rely on requires careful engineering and even more careful decision-making. We asked the SIG Apps chairs about the technical and operational trade-offs they weigh when introducing changes to Kubernetes’ core workload controllers. NF: What are some of the hardest technical or operational trade-offs SIG Apps encounters when evolving core workload controllers? MS: Honestly, a few tensions keep coming up: how aggressively a controller should give up on stuck pods, and what signals it actually needs to make that call correctly. At the same time, we always have to think about backward compatibility. Deployment, DaemonSet, and Job behavior has been depended on for a decade [by Kubernetes users, tooling, automation, and higher-level controllers], so even a change that’s clearly “more correct” can break automation people built around the old behavior without meaning to. JK: One of our hardest trade-offs is resisting the urge to make "elegant" design changes that break backward compatibility. Instead, we have to design opt-in features that let users adopt new behaviors without forcing them on legacy workloads. When we need to support completely new paradigms, we prefer introducing them as CRDs first rather than bloating the core APIs, like we are doing with Agent Sandbox, JobSet, and LWS. Looking ahead While much of SIG Apps’ work focuses on maintaining the stability of existing workload APIs, the group is also shaping the future of Kubernetes through new enhancements and proposals. We concluded by asking about one proposal that recently returned to active development and what it represents for the future of workload management. NF: The SIG recently discussed reviving KEP-4443 with a target release of Kubernetes 1.38. What opportunities or challenges does this proposal aim to address, and why is now the right time to revisit it? KEP-4443 addresses a small but real gap in the Job API: a PodFailurePolicy can be configured to add a condition reason to the JobFailed condition, but different pod failure policy rules targeting different container exit codes all produce that same generic reason. The proposal is simple: an optional Name field on each PodFailurePolicyRule, which gets appended to the JobFailed condition reason, so higher-level tools like JobSet can finally react differently depending on which rule triggered the failure. As for timing, the answer is as simple as it always is in open source: we lost the original contributor who was driving this. Now we’ve got someone new interested in picking it up, that’s why we’re targeting the next release. Getting Involved NF: For someone interested in contributing to SIG Apps, where would you recommend they start, especially if they are not yet a Kubernetes maintainer? MS: The best place to start is the #sig-apps slack channel and our regular SIG Apps meetings . We’ve all started there, and if it feels intimidating, or nobody replies right away, that’s completely normal. Everyone's busy. It's not personal. JK: In addition to what Maciej answered, I'd suggest looking at our newer subprojects and initiatives. Contributing to stable APIs like Deployment or StatefulSet can be daunting because the barrier for making changes is very high due to backward compatibility, and there is much less low-hanging fruit. If you are new to the community, projects like the Agent Sandbox are fantastic entry points. They are actively evolving, have a friendly group of maintainers, and offer plenty of greenfield development opportunities where you can make a significant impact quickly. Summary SIG Apps has shaped how Kubernetes applications are deployed and operated since the project’s earliest days. While users often interact with Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, and DaemonSets without thinking about the controllers behind them, the work within SIG Apps continues to shape the reliability and scalability of workloads across the Kubernetes ecosystem. From improving workload resilience and node lifecycle behavior to enabling new patterns for AI and distributed computing, the SIG is evolving Kubernetes while remaining committed to one of the project’s core principles: preserving the stability and backward compatibility that users depend on. Whether you’re interested in core workload APIs, emerging projects like Agent Sandbox, or helping improve the operational experience of Kubernetes users everywhere, SIG Apps offers many opportunities to get involved.
